title: Turn possibility into something real.
label: Welcome
deck: Build with AI. Think like an engineer. A hands-on journey from your first clear requirement to software you can explain, test, and improve.
tip: You don’t need to know every answer. Start by asking what evidence would convince you that an answer is right.
fact: This book follows one real project from CLI to web. You’ll study its mistakes as well as its working code.

title: Your workshop starts here.
label: Start here
deck: Set up a safe space to experiment. One working command is all you need to begin.
tip: Keep the reference project intact. Give every experiment its own folder and disposable history file.
fact: A virtual environment isolates Python packages. It does not isolate your files or protect a Git remote from an accidental push.

title: Name the transformation.
label: 01 · Requirements
deck: Turn an ambitious idea into a promise you can actually verify.
tip: Replace ‘make it better’ with a situation, an action, and an observable result.
fact: Acceptance criteria describe success. Acceptance tests provide evidence that those conditions hold.

title: Build the engine beneath the magic.
label: 02 · CLI & design
deck: Discover the small, clear boundaries that let a calculator grow without becoming a tangle.
tip: Before naming a pattern, explain the problem it solves. The name is a shortcut—not the justification.
fact: A plugin is a packaging and discovery mechanism. Its calculation algorithm plays the Strategy role.

title: Make confidence visible.
label: 03 · Testing
deck: Trade ‘it should work’ for evidence you can run, inspect, and trust within its limits.
tip: A red test is useful only when it fails for the behavior you intended to check.
fact: 100% statement coverage means the measured statements ran. It does not prove every requirement, input, or user experience.

title: Use it. Notice. Make it better.
label: 04 · Dogfooding
deck: Become your own first user—and turn friction into focused engineering improvements.
tip: Record what happened before explaining why. Observations and interpretations belong in different columns.
fact: The project’s first usability trial found missing command recall and unhelpful errors that passing arithmetic tests could not reveal.

title: One engine. A new doorway.
label: 05 · Web interface
deck: Bring your work into the browser with FastAPI and JavaScript, while keeping one source of mathematical truth.
tip: Trace a request from the browser all the way to a saved record. Don’t stop at a green status code.
fact: A server’s thread lock coordinates requests inside that process. It cannot coordinate a separate CLI writing the same CSV.

title: Own what you’ve created.
label: 06 · Engineering review
deck: Show your evidence, defend your decisions, and name the limits of what you know.
tip: Your strongest release statement is specific: ready for this user, this task, and these tested conditions.
fact: A tool attempt is not a verified outcome. Safari automation timed out in this case study, so Safari compatibility remains unverified.

title: Find the words. Understand the work.
label: Vocabulary
deck: Learn the language by connecting each term to real code, a real decision, and a common misconception.
tip: Try explaining a term without using the term itself. Then point to the code that makes it concrete.
fact: ‘Repository’ can mean a Git project or a persistence abstraction. The context changes the meaning.

title: Follow the evidence trail.
label: The real project
deck: Read the decisions, detours, and discoveries behind the calculator that became this book.
tip: Treat this story as a case to examine, not a perfect recipe to imitate. Good engineers question the reference, too.
fact: The historical 109-test reference is a dated snapshot—not a permanent guarantee about every future version.

title: Show understanding, not just output.
label: Assessment
deck: A transparent rubric rewards reasoning, meaningful tests, and honest evidence—not generated code volume.
tip: Read the rubric before you start. Use it to plan evidence, not to decorate a submission at the end.
fact: Proficiency requires 70 out of 100 points and a passing individual explanation. A polished artifact alone is not enough.

title: Help the next engineer find their spark.
label: For instructors
deck: Facilitate six sessions that turn AI assistance into an opportunity for deeper engineering judgment.
tip: Ask ‘what would change your mind?’ It invites learners to connect confidence with evidence.
fact: The materials have an author dry-run. No real learner pilot has been conducted yet; classroom effectiveness still needs observation.
